The Price of Choice in Selective Prediction

Daniel Cieślak ††thanks: Corresponding author: daniel.cieslak@pg.edu.pl Affiliation: Gdańsk University of Technology Affiliation: Gdańsk, Poland    Andrzej Czyżewski Affiliation: Gdańsk University of Technology Affiliation: Gdańsk, Poland
Abstract

A vendor may claim that some rule from a predeclared menu—a score threshold or a union of KK score intervals—lets its selective classifier keep a fraction κ\kappa of inputs while erring on at most a fraction α\alpha of them. Refuting such an existential claim means ruling out every permitted rule at once. The intersection–union test (IUT) does this without a multiplicity correction, but its sample cost as the menu grows, and how close that cost is to the best valid audit, are not captured by the level argument. We characterize both. For a fixed interior risk target α\alpha, menus of KK intervals and a risk gap γ\gamma, in the small-gap, large-menu regime of our theorem the minimax sample size at each fixed coverage floor κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1) is K⁡(1−κ)/(κ​γ2)K(1-\kappa)/(\kappa\gamma^{2}) up to logarithmic factors, and the exact IUT attains it: menu richness costs KK times the abstention odds, even though validity costs nothing. The lower bound holds for audits that know the score distribution; the upper bound extends to any menu of VC dimension dd. We then explain the linear cost. Every certificate that never rejects while some rule looks feasible on the audit data—the IUT, Bonferroni, DKW and uniform-convergence bounds—pays it even at laws where K/γ2\sqrt{K}/\gamma^{2} samples suffice, because the best-looking rule is optimistically biased. We then identify when the gap can and cannot be avoided: against constant-risk alternatives a reference-free audit reaches the testing scale, including the square-root rate on the sign family in its stated small-gap regime, whereas over a rich class with unknown heterogeneous risk the linear cost is unavoidable up to a logarithm. In simulation with K=4K=4, the raw menu cost changes 7.7-fold between κ=.5\kappa=.5 and .95.95; after dividing by the abstention odds and the theorem-motivated localized-VC logarithmic normalization used in Figure 1, the two endpoint values differ by about 5%. Held-out model families show that the same feasible-mixture mechanism is not confined to synthetic constructions: across three contemporary VLM judges, all 60 split-specific confidence-gate families have positive exact-hiding windows and 28/30 contracts selected on audit-A remain hidden on untouched audit-B; on the cleaner multi-annotator Polaris target, hiding persists on all 20 splits but is much narrower and transfers in 3/10 resplits. Frozen image and multimodal classifiers separately show boundary behavior consistent with the exact IUT guarantee and strong power relative to the practical certificates we compare.

1 Introduction

Before a selective classifier is deployed—in procurement, certification or a regulatory feasibility check—its vendor often claims that it can be configured to meet a standard: some permitted acceptance rule retains at least 90% of inputs while erring on at most 10% of the accepted ones. The menu of permitted rules is fixed in advance, for example thresholds on a confidence score or unions of a few score intervals. An auditor with fresh labeled data who wants to refute the claim cannot test one rule of its choice: showing that one rule fails leaves the vendor free to pick another. The null hypothesis is a union over the menu, and a rejection must rule out every rule at once. This is the dual of risk control and Learn-then-Test, which certify one rule selected by calibration (Chow, 1970; El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Bates et al., 2021; Angelopoulos et al., 2024; Angelopoulos et al., 2025).

The intersection–union test (IUT) is the natural audit: reject when every rule fails its own valid test. Because a true claim has one fixed witness rule, no multiplicity correction is needed (Berger, 1982; Berger and Hsu, 1996). This invites a tempting conclusion—that the size of the menu is free. It is not. We characterize the statistical price of menu richness, compare the exact IUT with the best valid audit, and identify assumptions under which the gap can close.

The main result in one line.

For menus of at most KK score intervals, a fixed interior risk target α\alpha, a fixed coverage floor κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1) and risk gap γ\gamma, the number of audit samples needed to refute every robustly false claim is

N≍1−κκ⏟abstention odds⋅Kγ2in the small-gap, large-menu regime, up to logarithmic factors,N\;\asymp\;\underbrace{\frac{1-\kappa}{\kappa}}_{\text{abstention odds}}\cdot\frac{K}{\gamma^{2}}\qquad\text{in the small-gap, large-menu regime, up to logarithmic factors,} (1)

and the exact IUT attains it (Theorem 1). This is the price of the menu, and it arises because the vendor’s freedom lies in which small part of the score line to abstain on (or, for κ<1/2\kappa<1/2, to accept): the auditor must rule out that the errors happen to be concentrated there, and the error mass of such a region fluctuates on the scale of that region, not of the whole sample. Richness is therefore cheap at high floors: at K=4K=4 in our simulations the menu cost at κ=.9\kappa=.9 is 4.4 times smaller than at κ=.5\kappa=.5 (Figure 1).

Contributions.

Table 1 summarizes the results; every lower bound holds for audits that are valid over the full, unrestricted null.

  1. 1.

    The abstention-odds law and optimality of the IUT (Section 3). For any menu of VC dimension dd the IUT needs O~​(d⁡(1−κ+γ)/(κ​γ2))\tilde{O}(d(1-\kappa+\gamma)/(\kappa\gamma^{2})) samples (Proposition 2); for unions of KK intervals, in the theorem’s small-gap regime, no valid audit, even one that knows the score distribution, needs fewer than Ω⁡(K⁡(1−κ)/(κ​γ2​log⁡K))\Omega(K(1-\kappa)/(\kappa\gamma^{2}\log K)) at any fixed floor κ\kappa (Theorem 1). The law covers the high floors used in practice (κ=.9\kappa=.9 in our experiments), where richness is several times cheaper than at κ=1/2\kappa=1/2.

  2. 2.

    A plug-in barrier (Section 4). We call a certificate EFC if it never rejects while some rule looks feasible on the audit data; the IUT, Bonferroni, DKW and uniform-convergence bounds all are. On explicit families with kk effective groups, every valid EFC certificate needs Ω⁡(k/γ2)\Omega(k/\gamma^{2}) samples at a law where Θ⁡(k/γ2)\Theta(\sqrt{k}/\gamma^{2}) suffice (Theorems 2 and 3), and this carries over to interval menus (Remark 1). The obstruction is a winner’s curse: the best empirical rule is optimistically biased by k/n\sqrt{k/n}.

  3. 3.

    What a better audit must know (Section 5). An unknown score distribution does not force the linear cost: against constant-risk alternatives, a reference-free audit valid for the unrestricted null reaches the testing scale and, on the uniform sign family in the stated small-gap regime, the square-root rate (Theorem 4). By contrast, uncertainty about heterogeneous conditional risk can force the linear cost up to a logarithm over the class of Theorem 5.

  4. 4.

    Evidence (Section 6). Simulations illustrate the coverage-floor dependence and the testing–estimation separation. Held-out families of frozen classifiers and VLM-judge confidence gates exhibit feasible-mixture hiding; on three VLM judges 28/30 audit-A midpoint contracts remain hidden on untouched audit-B, while a clean multi-annotator control retains positive but much smaller windows. Separate frozen-classifier audits show boundary behavior consistent with exact IUT level and strong finite-sample power against Bonferroni, DKW, total-loss and a valid non-EFC universal-inference audit.

For practitioners the message is short. Use the exact IUT: it needs no correction, runs in O⁡(M​K​n)O(MKn) time over MM score cells, and is minimax up to logarithms in the regime of Theorem 1. Within that regime, budget for the menu with (1): richness is cheap at high coverage floors and the menu penalty grows as the floor decreases. The held-out classifier and VLM-judge studies show why a family-level audit matters in practice: multiple individually failing gates can still hide the reference through feasible mixtures, while the constant-risk square-root shortcut requires additional structure.

Positioning and contributions.

Classical analyses of the IUT concern a fixed number of normal means (Lehmann, 1952; Berger, 1989); tests of many moment inequalities and reality checks have an intersection null and pay only log⁡K\log K (White, 2000; Chernozhukov et al., 2019); property testing of function classes separates known-distribution from distribution-free testing (Kearns and Ron, 2000; Blais et al., 2021). Our null is a union of convex sets of laws with a ratio-type risk constraint, validity is required over all of it, and the question is how the sample size depends on the menu. The lower-bound tools—mixture second moments, identity and independence testing, moment matching—are classical (Ingster, 1987; Valiant and Valiant, 2017; Diakonikolas and Kane, 2016; Cai and Low, 2011). Our contributions are the EFC barrier, the abstention-odds law, and three constructions they require: a padded moment-matching prior whose null draws stay existentially feasible while the alternative draws are robustly infeasible against every measurable set at any prescribed floor; a witness that controls the coverage screen and the risk simultaneously; and a localization of the IUT to the smaller side of the floor.

2 The audit problem

Observe i.i.d. pairs (S,L)(S,L) of score and binary loss. Freeze a measurable family 𝒜\mathcal{A} of acceptance rules (the menu) and a contract (κ,α)(\kappa,\alpha) independently of the audit sample. A law QQ is feasible if

∃A∈𝒜:cQ​(A)=Q⁡(S∈A)≥κ,rQ​(A)=Q⁡(L=1∣S∈A)≤α.\exists A\in\mathcal{A}:\quad c_{Q}(A)=Q(S\in A)\geq\kappa,\qquad r_{Q}(A)=Q(L=1\mid S\in A)\leq\alpha. (2)

Let ℋ⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{A}) be this existential null. It is unrestricted: score probabilities and conditional losses may both change. For a class 𝒫\mathcal{P} of infeasible laws, the minimax sample size is

N(𝒫,ℋ;δ,β)=inf{n≥1:∃ϕn∈[0,1],supQ∈ℋ𝔼Qnϕn≤δ,infP∈𝒫𝔼Pnϕn≥β}.N(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{H};\delta,\beta)=\inf\Big\{n\geq 1:\exists\phi_{n}\in[0,1],\ \sup_{Q\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbb{E}_{Q^{n}}\phi_{n}\leq\delta,\ \inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}_{P^{n}}\phi_{n}\geq\beta\Big\}. (3)

NIUTN_{\rm IUT} is the same quantity with ϕn\phi_{n} restricted to the exact IUT below. For a single law P0P_{0} we write N⁡(P0,ℋ)N(P_{0},\mathcal{H}); the optimal test may then use P0P_{0}, so this is an information benchmark as in local minimax testing (Balakrishnan and Wasserman, 2019). Larger classes 𝒫\mathcal{P} encode what the auditor does not know.

The exact IUT.

For a rule AA, let TAT_{A} and EAE_{A} count the audit observations it accepts and the accepted errors; TA∼Bin⁡(n,c⁡(A))T_{A}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,c(A)) and EA|TA=t∼Bin⁡(t,r⁡(A))E_{A}\mid T_{A}=t\sim\mathrm{Bin}(t,r(A)). Let UAU_{A} be the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound for coverage at error ζc\zeta_{c} and LAL_{A} the lower bound for risk at error ζr\zeta_{r} (Clopper and Pearson, 1934), and define the certified frontier

LIUT(𝒜,κ)=minA:UA≥κLA,min∅=+∞.L_{\rm IUT}(\mathcal{A},\kappa)=\min_{A:\,U_{A}\geq\kappa}L_{A},\qquad\min\varnothing=+\infty. (4)

It reads: with confidence 1−δ1-\delta, no permitted rule of coverage at least κ\kappa has risk below LIUTL_{\rm IUT}.

Proposition 1 (Validity without correction).

Rejecting feasibility when LIUT>αL_{\rm IUT}>\alpha has level at most ζc+ζr≤δ\zeta_{c}+\zeta_{r}\leq\delta over the unrestricted null.

Under the null a fixed population witness A∗A^{*} exists, and rejection requires failure of one of its two bounds. For unions of at most KK intervals over MM frozen score cells a dynamic program computes (4) exactly in O⁡(M​K​n)O(MKn) time (Appendix G). We use ζc=ζr=δ/2\zeta_{c}=\zeta_{r}=\delta/2.

Plug-in (EFC) certificates.

Call AA empirically feasible if TA≥κ​nT_{A}\geq\kappa n and EA≤α​TAE_{A}\leq\alpha T_{A}.

Definition 1 (EFC audits).

An audit ϕn\phi_{n} is empirical-feasibility consistent (EFC) if ϕn=0\phi_{n}=0 whenever some A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} is empirically feasible.

EFC audits never reject a claim that the vendor can apparently meet on the audit data itself, which makes their decisions easy to explain. Every certificate that screens with a coverage upper bound no smaller than the empirical coverage and rejects via risk lower bounds no larger than the empirical risk is EFC. This includes the IUT (for ζc,ζr≤1/2\zeta_{c},\zeta_{r}\leq 1/2), its Bonferroni variant, DKW and Rademacher uniform-convergence certificates, and the total-loss certificate (Appendix B.1). EFC plays the role of monotonicity in classical IUT theory (Perlman and Wu, 1999).

3 The abstention-odds law

For an arbitrary menu we place the power requirement on alternatives that are robustly infeasible:

𝒫γ​(𝒜)={P:rP​(A)≥α+γ​for every ​A∈𝒜​ with ​cP​(A)≥κ−γ}.\mathcal{P}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A})=\{P:\ r_{P}(A)\geq\alpha+\gamma\ \text{for every }A\in\mathcal{A}\text{ with }c_{P}(A)\geq\kappa-\gamma\}.

The class allows arbitrary score marginals and arbitrary, including informative, risk functions. The coverage slack γ\gamma excludes rules that sit just below the floor with very low risk, which no finite audit can resolve.

Proposition 2 (The IUT for every menu).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} have VC dimension dd, 0<δ<β<10<\delta<\beta<1, κ∈(0,1]\kappa\in(0,1], 0<γ≤κ/20<\gamma\leq\kappa/2 and α+γ≤1\alpha+\gamma\leq 1. For absolute constants CC: (i) the exact IUT has power at least β\beta uniformly over 𝒫γ​(𝒜)\mathcal{P}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}) once n≥C⁡{d+log⁡(2/δ)+log⁡(4/(1−β))}/(κ​γ)2n\geq C\{d+\log(2/\delta)+\log(4/(1-\beta))\}/(\kappa\gamma)^{2}; (ii) if some A0∈𝒜A_{0}\in\mathcal{A} has coverage at least κ\kappa under some score law, every valid audit needs n≥2​(β−δ)2​α​(1−α)/γ2n\geq 2(\beta-\delta)^{2}\alpha(1-\alpha)/\gamma^{2}; (iii) localization: the exact IUT has power at least β\beta over 𝒫γ​(𝒜)\mathcal{P}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}) whenever

n≥C​(1−κ+γ)​d​log⁡(2​e​n/d)+log⁡{8/(δ⁡(1−β))}κ​γ2.n\geq C\,\frac{(1-\kappa+\gamma)\,d\log(2en/d)+\log\{8/(\delta(1-\beta))\}}{\kappa\gamma^{2}}.

Part (i) combines VC uniform deviations with Clopper–Pearson inversion; part (ii) is a two-point bound (Appendix B.3). Part (iii) is the refinement that matters at high floors. A rule that passes the coverage screen differs from the whole score line only on a region of probability at most 1−κ+γ1-\kappa+\gamma, and it accepts at least a fraction κ/2\kappa/2 of the data. Writing its error mass as the overall error mass minus the error mass of the abstained region, only the latter varies over the menu. Relative (Bernstein-type) VC deviations bound it by (1−κ+γ)​d/n\sqrt{(1-\kappa+\gamma)d/n} up to logarithms, which for κ≥1/2\kappa\geq 1/2 is also the order of the risk error. When κ<1/2\kappa<1/2 the accepted region is the small side, its error mass fluctuates by κ​d/n\sqrt{\kappa d/n}, and dividing by κ\kappa gives d/(κ​n)\sqrt{d/(\kappa n)}; both cases are (1−κ+γ)​d/(κ​n)\sqrt{(1-\kappa+\gamma)d/(\kappa n)} up to a factor two. The Clopper–Pearson bounds adapt to both scales automatically, so the IUT needs no tuning.

For interval menus, the next result matches this dependence up to logarithmic factors at any fixed coverage floor.

Theorem 1 (Interval menus at any fixed coverage floor).

Let 𝒜K\mathcal{A}_{K} contain all unions of at most KK intervals of the score line, κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1), a∈(0,1/8]a\in(0,1/8], α∈[2​a,1−2​a]\alpha\in[2a,1-2a] and 0<δ<β<10<\delta<\beta<1. There are c,c′,C,K0>0c,c^{\prime},C,K_{0}>0 depending only on (a,δ,β)(a,\delta,\beta) such that for K≥K0K\geq K_{0} and γ≤c′​min⁡{κ,1−κ}/log⁡K\gamma\leq c^{\prime}\min\{\kappa,1-\kappa\}/\log K,

c​K​(1−κ)κ​γ2​log⁡K≤N⁡(𝒫γ​(𝒜K),ℋ)≤NIUT​(𝒫γ​(𝒜K))≤C⁡{K⁡(1−κ)​log⁡(e/(κ​γ))+1}κ​γ2.\frac{c\,K(1-\kappa)}{\kappa\gamma^{2}\log K}\;\leq\;N(\mathcal{P}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{K}),\mathcal{H})\;\leq\;N_{\rm IUT}(\mathcal{P}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{K}))\;\leq\;\frac{C\{K(1-\kappa)\log(e/(\kappa\gamma))+1\}}{\kappa\gamma^{2}}.

The lower bound holds even for audits that know the score distribution.

Thus, for every fixed κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1) in the stated small-gap regime, the IUT is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. Moreover, Proposition 2(i) gives O⁡(K/γ2)O(K/\gamma^{2}) at fixed κ\kappa, leaving only the log⁡K\log K gap to the lower bound. Proof idea. The lower bound embeds K−1K-1 consecutive score groups, each split into two halves whose losses are m±dbm\pm d_{b} with a random sign and a random magnitude dbd_{b}. Under the null and alternative priors the magnitudes match their first log⁡K\log K even moments but differ in their mean by the best polynomial approximation error of u\sqrt{u}, so the two mixtures are indistinguishable until n≳K/(γ2​log⁡K)n\gtrsim K/(\gamma^{2}\log K) (Theorem 5 below). To reach an arbitrary floor, a padding region carries the rest of the score mass: for κ≥1/2\kappa\geq 1/2 it has risk α\alpha and is accepted by every good rule, so only a fraction 2​(1−κ)2(1-\kappa) of the data is informative and the risk gap shrinks by (1−κ)/κ(1-\kappa)/\kappa; for κ<1/2\kappa<1/2 it has risk one and is never accepted. The delicate step is robust infeasibility: under the alternative prior every measurable set of coverage at least κ−γ\kappa-\gamma must have risk at least α+γ\alpha+\gamma, not only the menu’s rules. Because the conditional risk is piecewise constant, the least-risk sets fill the score line in increasing order of risk, and trimming them changes the risk by at most 2​γ​D/κ2\gamma D/\kappa (Appendix B.4).

Reading the law.

The menu cost K⁡(1−κ)/(κ​γ2)K(1-\kappa)/(\kappa\gamma^{2}) is a cost of power, not of validity: the level proof pays nothing for |𝒜||\mathcal{A}|, yet a richer menu gives the vendor more ways to place the abstained region where the audit sample happens to contain few errors. Part (i) holds for any uniform-convergence certificate with radius of order d/n\sqrt{d/n}; the endpoint DKW certificate (radius of order K/nK/\sqrt{n}) and policywise Bonferroni (of order K​log⁡M/n\sqrt{K\log M/n} over MM cells) have weaker guarantees, and part (iii) uses the Clopper–Pearson bounds’ adaptation to small proportions. The logarithmic gaps and constants remain open; at κ=1/2\kappa=1/2, with the constants of our proof, the new lower bound exceeds the elementary Ω⁡(K/γ2)\Omega(\sqrt{K}/\gamma^{2}) obstruction from Proposition 3 only for small γ\gamma and large KK. The next two sections explain why the cost is linear in KK and when an audit can avoid it.

4 A testing–estimation gap for existential audits

Sign families.

Fix p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), 0<γ<min⁡{p,1−p}0<\gamma<\min\{p,1-p\} and (κ,α)=(1/2,p−γ)(\kappa,\alpha)=(1/2,p-\gamma). The reference P0P_{0} has S∼Unif⁡[0,1]S\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1] and L|S∼Bern⁡(p)L\mid S\sim\Bern(p); it is infeasible. For positive weights ww in the simplex ΔB−1\Delta_{B-1}, partition [0,1][0,1] into groups GℓG_{\ell} of mass wℓw_{\ell}, each split into equal halves. Each θ∈{−1,+1}B\theta\in\{-1,+1\}^{B} accepts one half per group, giving 2B2^{B} rules AθA_{\theta}. A feasible component keeps the score law and sets

Qθ(L=1∣S=x)=p−γsθ(x),sθ(x)=1on Aθ,−1off Aθ.Q_{\theta}(L=1\mid S=x)=p-\gamma s_{\theta}(x),\qquad s_{\theta}(x)=1\ \text{on }A_{\theta},\ -1\ \text{off }A_{\theta}. (5)

Every component has coverage 1/21/2, accepted risk p−γp-\gamma, and the same distance from P0P_{0}; mixing them uniformly gives P0P_{0} exactly. All positive weight profiles share the same single-rule testing problems, incidence structure, VC dimension BB and growth function (Propositions 6–7); the families differ only in how their rules overlap. For the plateau profile with kk heavy groups, wℓ=(1−B−2)/kw_{\ell}=(1-B^{-2})/k for ℓ≤k\ell\leq k and the remaining mass B−2B^{-2} spread over the other groups, the effective dimension is deff=‖w‖2−2=k⁡{1+o⁡(1)}d_{\rm eff}=\|w\|_{2}^{-2}=k\{1+o(1)\}.

Theorem 2 (Testing scale).

Fix p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and 0<δ<β<10<\delta<\beta<1. If γ=γB<min⁡{p,1−p}\gamma=\gamma_{B}<\min\{p,1-p\} and B−2≤γB/16B^{-2}\leq\gamma_{B}/16, then as B→∞B\to\infty, uniformly in k≤Bk\leq B, the full-null sample size at the reference is N⁡(P0,ℋB,k,δ,β)=Θ⁡(k/γB2)N(P_{0},\mathcal{H}_{B,k};\delta,\beta)=\Theta(\sqrt{k}/\gamma_{B}^{2}).

The lower bound is Ingster’s second-moment method. For a prior Π\Pi over feasible components with 𝔼Π​Q=P0\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}Q=P_{0}, 1+χ2(𝔼ΠQn∥P0n)=𝔼Q,Q′∼Π[1+Ξ(Q,Q′)]n1+\chi^{2}(\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}Q^{n}\|P_{0}^{n})=\mathbb{E}_{Q,Q^{\prime}\sim\Pi}[1+\Xi(Q,Q^{\prime})]^{n} with Ξ=∫(𝑑Q/d​P0)​(d​Q′/d​P0)​d​P0−1\Xi=\int(dQ/dP_{0})(dQ^{\prime}/dP_{0})dP_{0}-1 (Lemma 3); here Ξ⁡(θ,θ′)=λ​∑ℓwℓ​θℓ​θℓ′\Xi(\theta,\theta^{\prime})=\lambda\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}\theta_{\ell}\theta^{\prime}_{\ell} with λ=γ2/[p⁡(1−p)]\lambda=\gamma^{2}/[p(1-p)], which gives:

Proposition 3 (Weight-profile obstruction).

Every level-δ\delta audit of a sign family has 𝔼P0n​ϕ≤δ+12​{exp⁡(n2​λ2​‖w‖22/2)−1}1/2\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}^{n}}\phi\leq\delta+\tfrac{1}{2}\{\exp(n^{2}\lambda^{2}\|w\|_{2}^{2}/2)-1\}^{1/2}, hence Nw=Ω⁡(deff/γ2)N_{w}=\Omega(\sqrt{d_{\rm eff}}/\gamma^{2}).

For the upper bound, every law of the full null—whether it changes scores, labels or both—is Ω⁡(γ)\Omega(\gamma)-far from P0P_{0} after pushing forward to the (4​k+2)(4k+2) half/label cells of the heavy groups, so identity testing needs O⁡(k/γ2)O(\sqrt{k}/\gamma^{2}) samples (Valiant and Valiant, 2017) (Appendix D).

Theorem 3 (The estimation cost of EFC audits).

Fix p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and 0<δ<β<10<\delta<\beta<1. There are γ0,c>0\gamma_{0},c>0 depending only on (p,δ,β)(p,\delta,\beta), and for each split below a C>0C>0, such that on the plateaus of Theorem 2, whenever γ≤γ0\gamma\leq\gamma_{0} and B−2≤γ/16B^{-2}\leq\gamma/16: (i) every level-δ\delta EFC audit has power below β\beta at P0P_{0} for all n≤c​k/γ2n\leq ck/\gamma^{2}; (ii) the exact IUT with any fixed split ζc+ζr=δ\zeta_{c}+\zeta_{r}=\delta, ζc,ζr∈(0,1/2]\zeta_{c},\zeta_{r}\in(0,1/2], has power at least β\beta for all n≥C​k/γ2n\geq Ck/\gamma^{2}. Hence NIUT=Θ⁡(k/γ2)N_{\rm IUT}=\Theta(k/\gamma^{2}) and NIUT/N⁡(P0,ℋB,k)=Θ⁡(k)N_{\rm IUT}/N(P_{0},\mathcal{H}_{B,k})=\Theta(\sqrt{k}).

Mechanism. In each heavy group choose the half containing more correct audit observations. Conditional on the correct observations and the error count, this rule accepts each error independently with probability 1/21/2, while its accepted correct count exceeds half of all correct observations by GG with 𝔼​G≳min⁡{n,n​k}\mathbb{E}G\gtrsim\min\{n,\sqrt{nk}\}. For n≪k/γ2n\ll k/\gamma^{2} this gain overwhelms the population gap n​γn\gamma and keeps the empirical coverage at least 1/21/2: a sample-dependent rule is empirically feasible, so no EFC audit rejects (Appendix C.2). Choosing the half with fewer errors would not control coverage. The optimal audit instead aggregates quadratic evidence whose fluctuation is k/n\sqrt{k}/n against a signal γ2\gamma^{2}. The EFC bound does not rely on the reference coverage sitting exactly at the floor: with qq-ary groups and reference coverage m/q>κm/q>\kappa it persists (Proposition 4, Appendix C.3).

Remark 1 (The barrier on interval menus).

Order the 2​K2K halves of the uniform sign family (k=B=Kk=B=K) along the score line, each group’s halves adjacent. Unions of at most KK intervals of these cells contain every sign rule, so Theorem 3(i) applies: for γ≤γ0\gamma\leq\gamma_{0}, every valid EFC audit of this interval menu needs Ω⁡(K/γ2)\Omega(K/\gamma^{2}) samples at P0P_{0}, without a logarithm, and the IUT needs O⁡(K/γ2)O(K/\gamma^{2}). Theorem 4 below gives a valid non-EFC audit with O⁡(K/γ2)O(\sqrt{K}/\gamma^{2}) samples at the same law for γ≤(2K)−1/4\gamma\leq(2K)^{-1/4}.

5 When can the gap be escaped?

The optimal audit of Theorem 2 knows P0P_{0}; the IUT knows nothing about it. Which missing knowledge forces the linear cost? Validity is always required over the unrestricted null; only the power requirement is placed on a class 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Let C1,…,CMC_{1},\ldots,C_{M} be score cells frozen independently of the audit sample and 𝒜\mathcal{A} any family of unions of cells.

Unknown score distribution, constant risk: a reference-free testing-scale audit.

Let 𝒫c​(α,γ)\mathcal{P}_{\rm c}(\alpha,\gamma) contain every law under which LL is independent of SS and P⁡(L=1)≥α+γP(L=1)\geq\alpha+\gamma, with an arbitrary score marginal.

Theorem 4 (Reference-free audit at the testing scale).

Fix κ∈(0,1]\kappa\in(0,1] and 0<δ<β<10<\delta<\beta<1. An audit that uses only cell labels and losses, and knows neither the score marginal nor P⁡(L=1)P(L=1), has level δ\delta over ℋ⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{A}) and power at least β\beta uniformly over 𝒫c​(α,γ)\mathcal{P}_{\rm c}(\alpha,\gamma) for every n≥Cδ,β​{M/(κ​γ)2+M2/3/(κ​γ)4/3}n\geq C_{\delta,\beta}\{\sqrt{M}/(\kappa\gamma)^{2}+M^{2/3}/(\kappa\gamma)^{4/3}\}. On the uniform sign family (M=2​kM=2k, κ=1/2\kappa=1/2) with γ≤(2k)−1/4\gamma\leq(2k)^{-1/4} this is Θ⁡(k/γ2)\Theta(\sqrt{k}/\gamma^{2}), while every valid EFC audit needs Ω⁡(k/γ2)\Omega(k/\gamma^{2}) at P0∈𝒫cP_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{\rm c}.

The audit rejects when the empirical loss rate exceeds α+γ/2\alpha+\gamma/2 and an independence tester for cell and loss (Diakonikolas and Kane, 2016) finds no dependence. The key fact is that feasibility forces dependence: if QQ has a witness AA and e=Q⁡(L=1)>αe=Q(L=1)>\alpha, every product law RR on cells and labels has TV⁡(Q,R)≥(e−α)​κ/3\TV(Q,R)\geq(e-\alpha)\kappa/3, because a product law assigns the witness the overall loss rate (Lemma 2). The audit is valid even for the family of all 2M2^{M} unions of cells, so it matches the testing scale only where that scale is M/γ2\sqrt{M}/\gamma^{2}; for small menus the IUT is better. It abstains whenever its independence test detects score–loss dependence. Section 6 separately reports strong score–loss dependence and held-out family-level hiding on frozen model outputs. The next result shows that, over a rich heterogeneous class, no valid audit can uniformly retain the square-root rate.

Unknown heterogeneous risk: the linear cost can be necessary.

Consider the uniform sign family with BB groups, κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 and the uniform score marginal, known to the auditor. For η∈[0,1]2​B\eta\in[0,1]^{2B} let PηP_{\eta} have loss probability ηb,h\eta_{b,h} on half hh of group bb; the best risk is r∗​(η)=B−1​∑bmin⁡{ηb,+,ηb,−}r^{*}(\eta)=B^{-1}\sum_{b}\min\{\eta_{b,+},\eta_{b,-}\}. Let 𝒫het(α,γ)={Pη:η∈[a,1−a]2​B,r∗(η)≥α+γ}\mathcal{P}_{\rm het}(\alpha,\gamma)=\{P_{\eta}:\eta\in[a,1-a]^{2B},\ r^{*}(\eta)\geq\alpha+\gamma\}.

Theorem 5 (The price of unknown heterogeneity).

Fix a∈(0,1/8]a\in(0,1/8], α∈[2​a,1−2​a]\alpha\in[2a,1-2a] and 0<δ<β<10<\delta<\beta<1. There are c1,c2,C,B0>0c_{1},c_{2},C,B_{0}>0 depending only on (a,δ,β)(a,\delta,\beta) such that for B≥B0B\geq B_{0} and γ≤c1/log⁡B\gamma\leq c_{1}/\log B, c2​B/(γ2​log⁡B)≤N⁡(𝒫het,ℋ)≤NIUT​(𝒫het)≤C​B/γ2c_{2}B/(\gamma^{2}\log B)\leq N(\mathcal{P}_{\rm het},\mathcal{H})\leq N_{\rm IUT}(\mathcal{P}_{\rm het})\leq CB/\gamma^{2}, whereas N⁡(P,ℋ)=O⁡(B/γ2)N(P,\mathcal{H})=O(\sqrt{B}/\gamma^{2}) for every single P∈𝒫hetP\in\mathcal{P}_{\rm het}.

The null and alternative priors set ηb,±=m±sb​db\eta_{b,\pm}=m\pm s_{b}d_{b} with a uniform sign sbs_{b} and a magnitude db∈[0,D]d_{b}\in[0,D] from ν0\nu_{0} or ν1\nu_{1}. These match 𝔼​d2​j\mathbb{E}d^{2j} for j≤L≍log⁡Bj\leq L\asymp\log B but differ in 𝔼​d\mathbb{E}d, and hence in r∗r^{*}, by twice the best degree-LL approximation error of u\sqrt{u} on [0,D2][0,D^{2}], of order D/LD/L (Bernstein, 1914; Lepski et al., 1999; Cai and Low, 2011). Under Poissonization the random signs make each group’s χ2\chi^{2} series depend only on the even moments, so all terms up to order LL cancel (Appendix B.5). Unlike ℓ1\ell_{1}-functional estimation (Jiao et al., 2018), the priors must keep the null draws existentially feasible. Together, Theorems 4 and 5 show that validity alone does not force the linear cost, while uncertainty about where the classifier errs can force it on a rich heterogeneous class.

6 Experiments

6.1 The abstention-odds law

We audit menus of K∈{1,2,4,8,16}K\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} intervals over M=64M=64 equal-mass score cells at floors κ∈{.5,.7,.8,.9,.95}\kappa\in\{.5,.7,.8,.9,.95\} (and .3.3 in Appendix H.4). The alternative has constant risk α+γ\alpha+\gamma (α=.10\alpha=.10, γ=.04\gamma=.04), so every rule has the same risk and the law lies in 𝒫γ\mathcal{P}_{\gamma} at every floor; any increase of the sample size with KK is therefore a pure cost of menu richness. For each (K,κ)(K,\kappa) the exact IUT audits 250 samples at each of 15 log-spaced sizes between 150 and 15,846, and we record the 80%-power crossing n80n_{80} and the menu cost n80​(K)−n80​(1)n_{80}(K)-n_{80}(1).

Figure 1 illustrates the coverage-floor dependence in Proposition 2(iii) and Theorem 1. The raw menu cost varies by almost an order of magnitude across floors. The right panel additionally divides by the theorem-motivated localized-VC logarithmic factor discussed in Appendix B.3; that factor is not used in the proofs, and the resulting variation is substantially reduced until the menu saturates. The flattening itself is the localization mechanism at work: only rules that differ on the small abstained region compete. The IUT’s level is not at issue here (it is exact); boundary checks are reported below.

6.2 Sign families: the IUT against the information envelope

We fix B=256B=256 (22562^{256} rules), p=.25p=.25, κ=.5\kappa=.5, k∈{1,4,16,64,256}k\in\{1,4,16,64,256\} and γ∈{.04,.02}\gamma\in\{.04,.02\}. The exact dynamic program audits 1,500 samples per grid point. The comparator is the Neyman–Pearson curve for P0nP_{0}^{n} against the uniform feasible mixture; its population version bounds the power of every valid audit, so it is an information envelope, not an audit.

At γ=.04\gamma=.04 the IUT’s crossing rises from 2,342 to 32,796 samples as kk grows from 1 to 256, and the envelope’s from 1,001 to 7,384; halving the gap multiplies all crossings by 3.91–4.17. Fitting γ2​n80≈a0+a1​k+a2​k\gamma^{2}n_{80}\approx a_{0}+a_{1}\sqrt{k}+a_{2}k gives a2≈0.13a_{2}\approx 0.13 for the IUT at both gaps and a2≈0a_{2}\approx 0 for the envelope, as Theorems 2–3 predict. Ten boundary-null checks, one per (k,γ)(k,\gamma) with 20,000 audits each, give rejection rates of 0–4.7%. Across the simulated kk values the gap to the envelope is a factor of 2.2–4.4. In the separate fixed-degree (L=2L=2) heterogeneity-envelope experiment, the heterogeneous envelope overtakes the known-reference one only at B≈2.6×105B\approx 2.6\times 10^{5} (Appendix B.7).

6.3 Auditing the auditors: VLM-judge reliability

Automated VLM judges are increasingly used to automate evaluation, and a reliability claim is naturally existential: some confidence gate should retain enough evaluations while keeping serious judge errors below a target. We use the public score-token log-probabilities and human scores released by Kumar et al. (2026). For each item let L=𝟏{|y^−yhuman|>1}L=\mathbf{1}\{|\hat{y}-y_{\rm human}|>1\}, matching the source study’s ±1\pm 1 scoring criterion; a non-1–5 parse is counted as a serious error, with a drop-invalid sensitivity analysis in the Supplementary Note. From the five score-token probabilities we predeclare three label-free confidence channels—maximum probability, negative entropy and top-two margin—and cross each with target coverages .65.65 and .90.90, giving six gates at contract floor κ=.60\kappa=.60.

For each judge we use ten deterministic three-way resplits. Thresholds are frozen from calibration scores only; audit-A selects the midpoint of its exact fixed-marginal hiding window I=[αH,αind)I=[\alpha_{H},\alpha_{\rm ind}), and untouched audit-B tests transfer. Thus Whide>0W_{\rm hide}>0 means no individual gate is feasible at some target even though feasible alternatives can convexify to the empirical reference. Table 2 reports the result.

On MLLM-Judge, every one of the 60 split-specific windows is positive and 28/30 midpoint contracts transfer. To test whether this is merely noisy single-annotator supervision, we repeat the same LLaVA-Critic protocol on Polaris, where the released target averages at least three annotators and the same judge is much more accurate (Kumar et al., 2026). All 20 windows remain positive, but the median held-out width falls from 4.97 to 0.33 percentage points and midpoint transfer falls from 10/10 to 3/10. On a representative Polaris audit-B split, singleton families have zero window, 60% of two-gate and 90% of three-gate subfamilies hide, and every subfamily of size at least four hides (Supplementary Note). The mechanism therefore persists under cleaner supervision, while its magnitude and split stability are population dependent. These are finite-target mechanism diagnostics, not an instance-specific minimax verification of Theorem 5.

6.4 Frozen classifier certificates and family geometry

We also treat frozen classifier outputs as populations: CIFAR-10/100 ResNet-18, ImageNetV2 ViT-B/16 and CMU-MOSEI MLP outputs (Krizhevsky, 2009; Recht et al., 2019; Bagher Zadeh et al., 2018). Calibration fixes score cells and the audit half supplies labels. At κ=.9\kappa=.9, the exact IUT has no observed boundary rejection above 1.8% and is the most powerful certificate compared except for one n=500n=500 CIFAR-100 point within Monte Carlo error; Bonferroni needs several times more data, structured DKW is vacuous here, and a score-agnostic total-loss certificate fails when total error is small relative to 1−κ1-\kappa (Table 8, Appendix H.2).

The constant-risk premise of Theorem 4 is strongly contradicted: a cell–loss independence diagnostic rejects in every one of 200 audits of size 500 on each population. More directly, a separate six-policy, three-way held-out geometry experiment freezes gates from calibration scores only. All 60 audit-A and all 60 audit-B windows are positive; 47/60 midpoint contracts selected on A transfer to untouched B. Singleton subfamilies have zero hiding, 96.7% of pairs hide, and every subfamily of size at least three hides (Supplementary Note, Section S5). Thus the same feasible-mixture mechanism appears on standard classifier families, without claiming that these populations instantiate Theorem 5’s asymptotic hard class.

Finally, as a valid non-EFC reference-free competitor we implement cross-fit universal inference (Wasserman et al., 2020). It has no observed boundary rejections, but at Δ=.05\Delta=.05 its first 80%-power grid point is n=10,000n=10{,}000–50,00050{,}000, versus 500–2,500 for the IUT; at Δ=.02\Delta=.02 it does not reach 80% power by 50,00050{,}000 (Table 12, Appendix H.5). This evaluates one practical non-EFC construction, not all non-EFC audits.

7 Related work and limitations

Risk control, Learn-then-Test and Pareto testing certify selected rules (Bates et al., 2021; Angelopoulos et al., 2024; Angelopoulos et al., 2025; Laufer-Goldshtein et al., 2023); model falsification, subgroup auditing and PAC verification address adjacent goals (Müller et al., 2025; Cherian and Candès, 2024; Mutreja and Shafer, 2026). Intersection–union validity is classical (Berger, 1982; Berger and Hsu, 1996; Lehmann and Romano, 2005); for a fixed number of normal means the IUT is the likelihood-ratio test and non-monotone tests can be uniformly more powerful (Lehmann, 1952; Berger, 1989), at the price of non-monotone rejection regions that can yield counterintuitive inferences (Perlman and Wu, 1999). Moment-inequality and intersection-bound tests (Andrews and Soares, 2010; Chernozhukov et al., 2013; Romano et al., 2014; Bugni et al., 2015) ask whether some parameter satisfies a set of inequalities; with many inequalities, as in reality checks (White, 2000; Hansen, 2005), the cost is logarithmic in their number (Chernozhukov et al., 2019) because that null is an intersection, whereas ours is a union. Inference on winners corrects the selection bias of an empirical optimum (Andrews et al., 2024), the bias that EFC certificates do not correct; sequential tests of whether some arm lies below a threshold address a related existential question (Kaufmann et al., 2018); confidence sequences give anytime versions of the IUT (Howard et al., 2021) (Appendix G). Universal inference gives reference-free composite tests (Wasserman et al., 2020); recent work on testable hypotheses and safe anytime-valid inference provides broader characterizations and tools for composite testing (Larsson et al., 2026b; Ramdas et al., 2023). In property testing, unions of dd intervals are testable from O⁡(d)O(\sqrt{d}) samples when the input distribution is known but need Ω⁡(d/log⁡d)\Omega(d/\log d) distribution-free (Kearns and Ron, 2000; Balcan et al., 2012; Blais et al., 2021); related interval and flat structure also appears in identity testing of structured distributions (Diakonikolas et al., 2015), and optimal risk can be estimated faster than learned (Kong and Valiant, 2018). Minimax L1L_{1}-distance estimation and tolerant distribution testing exhibit related linear-over-log sample-complexity phenomena (Jiao et al., 2018; Canonne et al., 2022). Recent work studies calibrated uncertainty for VLM judges and releases the score-token features used in our auditing application (Kumar et al., 2026). Our null is a union of convex sets of laws with ratio-type constraints, losses are noisy, and an unknown input distribution alone does not force the linear scale (Theorem 4), whereas unknown conditional risk can force it on the heterogeneous class of Theorem 5. The Supplementary Note relates the one-observation geometry to convex-set testing (Goldenshluger et al., 2015).

Limitations.

Losses are binary, the contract has one coverage floor, and data are i.i.d.; distribution shift is outside our scope. For each fixed coverage floor, the interval-menu bounds are worst-case and match up to logarithms in the stated small-gap, large-KK regime; the lower bound is asymptotic in KK; the sharp testing–estimation spectrum and the constant-risk result are proved on sign families; an Ω⁡(d)\Omega(d) bound for every VC-dd family is open. Theorem 4 is an existence result with an untuned tester. The natural-family and VLM-judge studies are finite-target mechanism diagnostics, not instance-specific minimax lower bounds for Theorem 5; the six VLM gates are illustrative and use released benchmark outputs rather than production traffic. The non-EFC experiment evaluates one universal-inference construction rather than all possible non-EFC audits. Nonrejection certifies no rule.

AI use statement

Generative AI was used to improve the clarity and presentation of manuscript claims, assist with software implementation and debugging, and provide critical feedback on claims and arguments during manuscript development. AI-generated suggestions were treated as editorial and technical assistance rather than as evidence or independent validation. The authors are fully responsible for the final claims, proofs, code, citations, analyses, and submission.

Ethics statement

The empirical studies reuse frozen benchmark model outputs and released human annotations and collect no new human-subject data. The work concerns statistical auditability and does not introduce a clinical decision system or an automated evaluator for deployment. Population interpretations require a sampling model appropriate to the intended setting.

Reproducibility statement

The supplement contains this manuscript’s figures, analysis scripts, exact rational certificates, frozen internal inputs, and derived VLM-audit summaries; the public third-party VLM feature files are referenced by source and are not redistributed. The analyses for Section 5 and Figure 3 are provided with their tests. The release README maps claims to code and distinguishes recomputed results from retained outputs. Appendix H and the Supplementary Note give protocols and limitations.

Appendix A Roadmap and notation

Local notation.

A few symbols are reused locally with meanings fixed by context: LL is the loss, but the polynomial degree in Theorem 5; MM is the number of cells, but the error count in the proofs of Theorem 3 and Proposition 4; mm is a prior midpoint in Theorem 5 and the number of selected parts in the qq-ary construction; KK counts intervals, and K⁡(Q,Q′)K(Q,Q^{\prime}) is the overlap kernel of Lemma 3; λ\lambda is γ2/[p⁡(1−p)]\gamma^{2}/[p(1-p)] in Section 4 and a Poisson mean in Appendix B.5.

Where the main results are proved.

This appendix contains everything the main theorems use. EFC certificates, Theorem 4, Proposition 2 (including the localization in part (iii)), Theorem 1 (Appendix B.4) and Theorem 5: Appendix B. Theorem 3, the Rademacher formula and Proposition 5: Appendix C. Theorem 2 and Propositions 6, 3 and 7: Appendix D. Lemma 3: Appendix E. Proposition 1 and the dynamic programs: Appendix G. The witness power ceiling (Corollary 3) and the collision bound (Theorem 6): Appendix F. Experimental protocols and all tables, including the abstention-odds simulation and the universal-inference audit: Appendix H. A separate Supplementary Note in the supplementary material collects one-observation geometry (exact projections, Hall–TV formulas, the eight-atom pairwise example and natural hiding windows) that the main theorems do not use.

Appendix B EFC certificates, reference-free testing, and unknown heterogeneity

B.1 Which certificates are EFC

Lemma 1 (Clopper–Pearson bounds bracket the empirical proportion).

Let X∼Bin⁡(t,q)X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(t,q) with observed value xx. For ζ≤1/2\zeta\leq 1/2 the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound at error ζ\zeta is at least x/tx/t and the lower bound is at most x/tx/t.

Proof.

When the mean t​qtq is an integer, it is a median of Bin⁡(t,q)\mathrm{Bin}(t,q) (Kaas and Buhrman, 1980). At q=x/tq=x/t we therefore have Pq​(X≤x)≥1/2≥ζP_{q}(X\leq x)\geq 1/2\geq\zeta and Pq​(X≥x)≥1/2≥ζP_{q}(X\geq x)\geq 1/2\geq\zeta. The upper bound is the largest qq with Pq​(X≤x)≥ζP_{q}(X\leq x)\geq\zeta, so it is at least x/tx/t; the lower bound is symmetric. ∎

Let AA be empirically feasible: TA≥κ​nT_{A}\geq\kappa n and EA≤α​TAE_{A}\leq\alpha T_{A}.

  • •

    Exact IUT and policywise Bonferroni. By Lemma 1, UA≥TA/n≥κU_{A}\geq T_{A}/n\geq\kappa, so AA passes the coverage screen, and LA≤EA/TA≤αL_{A}\leq E_{A}/T_{A}\leq\alpha. Hence LIUT≤αL_{\rm IUT}\leq\alpha and the audit does not reject. Bonferroni replaces ζ\zeta by ζ/|𝒜|≤1/2\zeta/|\mathcal{A}|\leq 1/2 and is covered by the same argument.

  • •

    DKW and Rademacher certificates (Appendices G.5–G.6). Their screen cn​(A)≥κ−ϵc_{n}(A)\geq\kappa-\epsilon is passed by AA, and their lower bound [mn​(A)−ϵ]+/min⁡{1,cn​(A)+ϵ}[m_{n}(A)-\epsilon]_{+}/\min\{1,c_{n}(A)+\epsilon\} is at most mn​(A)/cn​(A)=EA/TA≤αm_{n}(A)/c_{n}(A)=E_{A}/T_{A}\leq\alpha.

  • •

    Total-loss certificate. Writing e^\hat{e} for the empirical loss rate, e^≤(EA+n−TA)/n≤1−(1−α)​TA/n≤1−κ⁡(1−α)\hat{e}\leq(E_{A}+n-T_{A})/n\leq 1-(1-\alpha)T_{A}/n\leq 1-\kappa(1-\alpha). Hence (e^+κ−1)/κ≤α(\hat{e}+\kappa-1)/\kappa\leq\alpha; its lower confidence version is smaller by Lemma 1, so it does not reject.

Part (i) of Theorem 3 therefore applies to every certificate compared in Section 6.

B.2 Proof of Theorem 4

Throughout, laws are identified with their pushforwards to [M]×{0,1}[M]\times\{0,1\} (cell index and loss). This loses nothing for the null: every A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} is a union of cells, so the contract depends on QQ only through this pushforward, and the pushforward of a feasible law is feasible for the induced family. Products on the original space push forward to products.

Lemma 2 (Feasibility forces dependence).

Let QQ be feasible with witness AA, and let e=Q⁡(L=1)>αe=Q(L=1)>\alpha. Then TV⁡(Q,R)≥(e−α)​Q​(A)/3\TV(Q,R)\geq(e-\alpha)Q(A)/3 for every product law R=ν⊗Bern⁡(q)R=\nu\otimes\Bern(q) on [M]×{0,1}[M]\times\{0,1\}.

Proof.

Let t=TV⁡(Q,R)t=\TV(Q,R). If t≥et\geq e or t≥Q⁡(A)t\geq Q(A) the claim holds because (e−α)​Q​(A)/3<min⁡{e,Q⁡(A)}(e-\alpha)Q(A)/3<\min\{e,Q(A)\}. Otherwise, comparing the events {L=1}\{L=1\}, {S∈A}\{S\in A\} and {S∈A,L=1}\{S\in A,L=1\} gives q≥e−tq\geq e-t, ν⁡(A)≥Q⁡(A)−t\nu(A)\geq Q(A)-t and q​ν​(A)≤Q⁡(A,L=1)+t≤α​Q​(A)+tq\nu(A)\leq Q(A,L=1)+t\leq\alpha Q(A)+t. Thus α​Q​(A)+t≥(e−t)​(Q⁡(A)−t)≥e​Q​(A)−t⁡(e+Q⁡(A))≥e​Q​(A)−2​t\alpha Q(A)+t\geq(e-t)(Q(A)-t)\geq eQ(A)-t(e+Q(A))\geq eQ(A)-2t, so 3​t≥(e−α)​Q​(A)3t\geq(e-\alpha)Q(A). ∎

Independence tester.

For distributions on [M]×[2][M]\times[2], Diakonikolas and Kane (2016) give a tester that, from O⁡(M/ϵ2+M2/3/ϵ4/3)O(\sqrt{M}/\epsilon^{2}+M^{2/3}/\epsilon^{4/3}) samples, accepts every product law and rejects every law ϵ\epsilon-far in total variation from all product laws, each with probability at least 2/32/3 (their ℓ1\ell_{1} parameter is 2​ϵ2\epsilon). Taking the majority of O⁡(log⁡(1/ϵ′))O(\log(1/\epsilon^{\prime})) independent runs reduces both error probabilities to ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime}. Denote the amplified output by Ψ∈{0,1}\Psi\in\{0,1\}, with Ψ=1\Psi=1 meaning “dependent”.

The audit.

Let ϵ′=min⁡{δ,(1−β)/2}\epsilon^{\prime}=\min\{\delta,(1-\beta)/2\} and ϵ=κ​γ/12\epsilon=\kappa\gamma/12. Reject feasibility if and only if e^≥α+γ/2\hat{e}\geq\alpha+\gamma/2 and Ψ=0\Psi=0, where e^\hat{e} is the empirical loss rate and Ψ\Psi uses the independence tester at distance ϵ\epsilon and error ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime}. Neither the score marginal nor P⁡(L=1)P(L=1) is an input. Let n0n_{0} be the larger of 8​log⁡(1/ϵ′)/γ28\log(1/\epsilon^{\prime})/\gamma^{2} and the amplified tester’s sample size; for n<n0n<n_{0} the audit does not reject, and for n≥n0n\geq n_{0} it applies the rule above to the first n0n_{0} observations for the tester.

Let Q∈ℋ⁡(𝒜)Q\in\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{A}) and e=Q⁡(L=1)e=Q(L=1). If e≤α+γ/4e\leq\alpha+\gamma/4, Hoeffding’s inequality gives Q(e^≥α+γ/2)≤exp(−nγ2/8)≤ϵ′Q(\hat{e}\geq\alpha+\gamma/2)\leq\exp(-n\gamma^{2}/8)\leq\epsilon^{\prime} once n≥8​log⁡(1/ϵ′)/γ2n\geq 8\log(1/\epsilon^{\prime})/\gamma^{2}. With M=2​kM=2k and κ=1/2\kappa=1/2, M2/3γ−4/3≤M1/2γ−2M^{2/3}\gamma^{-4/3}\leq M^{1/2}\gamma^{-2} if and only if γ≤M−1/4\gamma\leq M^{-1/4}, so N⁡(𝒫c,ℋ)=O⁡(k/γ2)N(\mathcal{P}_{\rm c},\mathcal{H})=O(\sqrt{k}/\gamma^{2}) in that regime. B.3 Proof of Proposition 2

Two inversions.

For X∼Bin⁡(t,q)X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(t,q) observed at xx, Hoeffding’s inequality inverted at error ζ\zeta gives that the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound is at most x/t+log⁡(1/ζ)/(2​t)x/t+\sqrt{\log(1/\zeta)/(2t)} and the lower bound is at least x/t−log⁡(1/ζ)/(2​t)x/t-\sqrt{\log(1/\zeta)/(2t)}.

Uniform deviations.

The classes ℱ1={(s,l)↦𝟏A​(s):A∈𝒜}\mathcal{F}_{1}=\{(s,l)\mapsto\mathbf{1}_{A}(s):A\in\mathcal{A}\} and ℱ2={(s,l)↦l​ 1A​(s):A∈𝒜}\mathcal{F}_{2}=\{(s,l)\mapsto l\,\mathbf{1}_{A}(s):A\in\mathcal{A}\} have VC dimension at most dd; a set shattered by ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} consists of points with l=1l=1 whose scores are shattered by 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The VC bound for Boolean classes (Vershynin, 2018, Chapter 8) gives 𝔼​supf∈ℱi|Pn​f−P​f|≤C0​d/n\mathbb{E}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{i}}|P_{n}f-Pf|\leq C_{0}\sqrt{d/n}, and the bounded-differences inequality gives, with probability at least 1−(1−β)/21-(1-\beta)/2 for both classes simultaneously,

supA∈𝒜|cn​(A)−c⁡(A)|≤ϵn,supA∈𝒜|mn​(A)−m⁡(A)|≤ϵn,\displaystyle\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}}|c_{n}(A)-c(A)|\leq\epsilon_{n},\qquad\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}}|m_{n}(A)-m(A)|\leq\epsilon_{n},
ϵn=C0​d/n+log⁡(8/(1−β))/(2​n),\displaystyle\epsilon_{n}=C_{0}\sqrt{d/n}+\sqrt{\log(8/(1-\beta))/(2n)},

where cn​(A)=TA/nc_{n}(A)=T_{A}/n, m⁡(A)=P⁡(S∈A,L=1)m(A)=P(S\in A,L=1) and mn​(A)=EA/nm_{n}(A)=E_{A}/n.

Part (i).

Let P∈𝒫γ​(𝒜)P\in\mathcal{P}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}) and work on the event above. Suppose AA passes the coverage screen, UA≥κU_{A}\geq\kappa. By the first inversion cn​(A)≥κ−log⁡(2/δ)/(2​n)c_{n}(A)\geq\kappa-\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}, so c⁡(A)≥κ−log⁡(2/δ)/(2​n)−ϵn≥κ−γc(A)\geq\kappa-\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}-\epsilon_{n}\geq\kappa-\gamma provided log⁡(2/δ)/(2​n)+ϵn≤γ\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}+\epsilon_{n}\leq\gamma. The definition of 𝒫γ\mathcal{P}_{\gamma} then gives m⁡(A)≥(α+γ)​c​(A)m(A)\geq(\alpha+\gamma)c(A), and since c⁡(A)≥κ−γ≥κ/2c(A)\geq\kappa-\gamma\geq\kappa/2,

EATA≥m⁡(A)−ϵnc⁡(A)+ϵn≥α+γ−2​ϵnc⁡(A)≥α+γ−4​ϵnκ.\frac{E_{A}}{T_{A}}\geq\frac{m(A)-\epsilon_{n}}{c(A)+\epsilon_{n}}\geq\alpha+\gamma-\frac{2\epsilon_{n}}{c(A)}\geq\alpha+\gamma-\frac{4\epsilon_{n}}{\kappa}.

If also ϵn≤κ/4\epsilon_{n}\leq\kappa/4, then TA≥n​κ/4T_{A}\geq n\kappa/4, and the second inversion gives LA≥α+γ−4​ϵn/κ−2​log⁡(2/δ)/(n​κ)L_{A}\geq\alpha+\gamma-4\epsilon_{n}/\kappa-\sqrt{2\log(2/\delta)/(n\kappa)}. All three conditions, and LA>αL_{A}>\alpha, hold once n≥C⁡{d+log⁡(2/δ)+log⁡(4/(1−β))}/(κ​γ)2n\geq C\{d+\log(2/\delta)+\log(4/(1-\beta))\}/(\kappa\gamma)^{2} for an absolute CC. Then every screened policy has LA>αL_{A}>\alpha, and if no policy is screened LIUT=+∞L_{\rm IUT}=+\infty; either way the IUT rejects. Its power is at least 1−(1−β)/2≥β1-(1-\beta)/2\geq\beta.

Part (ii).

Choose a score law under which c⁡(A0)≥κc(A_{0})\geq\kappa and let PP have constant risk α+γ\alpha+\gamma. Every policy has risk α+γ\alpha+\gamma, so P∈𝒫γ​(𝒜)P\in\mathcal{P}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}). Let QQ equal PP except that the risk inside A0A_{0} is α\alpha; then A0A_{0} witnesses feasibility of QQ. B.4 Proof of Theorem 1

Upper bound.

Unions of at most KK intervals have VC dimension d=2​Kd=2K. Part (iii) of Proposition 2 with 1−κ+γ≤2​(1−κ)1-\kappa+\gamma\leq 2(1-\kappa) (as γ≤1−κ\gamma\leq 1-\kappa) gives power at least β\beta once n≥C⁡{K⁡(1−κ)​log⁡(2​e​n/K)+1}/(κ​γ2)n\geq C\{K(1-\kappa)\log(2en/K)+1\}/(\kappa\gamma^{2}), with CC depending on (δ,β)(\delta,\beta). Fix B=K−1B=K-1 and let γ4\gamma_{4}, DD, mm, LL, ν0,ν1\nu_{0},\nu_{1} be as in Steps 1–2 of the proof of Theorem 5 with this BB; the conditions imposed below imply those of that theorem. Scores are uniform on [0,1][0,1]. A construction region RR of mass π\pi is split into BB consecutive groups of mass π/B\pi/B, each split into a left and a right half, with loss probability ηb,±=m±sb​db\eta_{b,\pm}=m\pm s_{b}d_{b} on the two halves as in Step 2. Its complement, the padding, has a fixed conditional loss probability ηpad\eta_{\rm pad} that is the same under both priors. The inner best risk is rin∗​(η)=m−B−1​∑bdbr^{*}_{\rm in}(\eta)=m-B^{-1}\sum_{b}d_{b}, and the lower halves (those with risk m−dbm-d_{b}) have total mass π/2\pi/2. We distinguish two cases.

Case κ≥1/2\kappa\geq 1/2. Take π=2​(1−κ)\pi=2(1-\kappa), padding F=[0,1−π)F=[0,1-\pi) with ηpad=α\eta_{\rm pad}=\alpha, and R=[1−π,1]R=[1-\pi,1]. The set WW formed by FF and the lower halves has coverage 1−π+π/2=κ1-\pi+\pi/2=\kappa, is a union of at most B+1=KB+1=K intervals, and has risk

r⁡(W)=α+π2​κ​{rin∗​(η)−α}=α+1−κκ​{rin∗​(η)−α}.r(W)=\alpha+\tfrac{\pi}{2\kappa}\{r^{*}_{\rm in}(\eta)-\alpha\}=\alpha+\tfrac{1-\kappa}{\kappa}\{r^{*}_{\rm in}(\eta)-\alpha\}.

Every upper half has risk m+db≥mm+d_{b}\geq m, and every point of WW has risk at most mm, because m−α=𝔼ν0​d−g/4≥3​g/4>0m-\alpha=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{0}}d-g/4\geq 3g/4>0. Case κ<1/2\kappa<1/2. Take π=2​κ\pi=2\kappa, R=[0,π)R=[0,\pi) and padding H=[π,1]H=[\pi,1] with ηpad=1\eta_{\rm pad}=1. Indistinguishability.

Poissonize as in Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 5, with mean n′n^{\prime}. Counts in the padding are independent of counts in RR and have the same law under both priors, so the total variation between the two mixtures equals that between the mixtures of the RR-counts. These are independent Poisson counts with means λ​ηb,h\lambda\eta_{b,h} and λ⁡(1−ηb,h)\lambda(1-\eta_{b,h}) in each half, now with λ=π​n′/(2​B)\lambda=\pi n^{\prime}/(2B), so Steps 4–6 apply verbatim with ρ=π​n′/{B​m​(1−m)}\rho=\pi n^{\prime}/\{Bm(1-m)\}. The condition τ=ρ​D2≤(2​L+2)/e3\tau=\rho D^{2}\leq(2L+2)/e^{3} holds whenever π​n′≤c​B/(γ42​log⁡B)\pi n^{\prime}\leq c\,B/(\gamma_{4}^{2}\log B). In the case κ≥1/2\kappa\geq 1/2 this reads n′≤c​B​(1−κ)/(8​κ2​γ2​log⁡B)n^{\prime}\leq c\,B(1-\kappa)/(8\kappa^{2}\gamma^{2}\log B), and in the case κ<1/2\kappa<1/2 it reads n′≤c​B/(8​κ​γ2​log⁡B)n^{\prime}\leq c\,B/(8\kappa\gamma^{2}\log B). Both are at least c′′​K​(1−κ)/(κ​γ2​log⁡K)c^{\prime\prime}K(1-\kappa)/(\kappa\gamma^{2}\log K) for K≥3K\geq 3. Hence no valid audit with fewer samples has power β\beta over 𝒫γ​(𝒜K)\mathcal{P}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{K}).

Conditions.

Theorem 5 needs γ4≤c1/log⁡B\gamma_{4}\leq c_{1}/\log B, the case κ<1/2\kappa<1/2 needs D≤κ/2D\leq\kappa/2, and D=γ4/EL≤γ4​L/c∗D=\gamma_{4}/E_{L}\leq\gamma_{4}L/c_{*} with L=⌈log⁡B⌉L=\lceil\log B\rceil. In the case κ≥1/2\kappa\geq 1/2, γ4=2​κ​γ/(1−κ)≤2​γ/(1−κ)\gamma_{4}=2\kappa\gamma/(1-\kappa)\leq 2\gamma/(1-\kappa); in the case κ<1/2\kappa<1/2, γ4=2​γ\gamma_{4}=2\gamma. All conditions therefore hold when γ≤c′​min⁡{κ,1−κ}/log⁡K\gamma\leq c^{\prime}\min\{\kappa,1-\kappa\}/\log K for a suitable c′c^{\prime} depending only on aa, and K≥K0K\geq K_{0}. The auditor may know the uniform score marginal, the cells and the padding: only the location and size of the risk heterogeneity inside RR are random. At κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 the padding is empty and the construction is the one of Theorem 5 with B=K−1B=K-1 consecutive groups. ∎

Numerical checks.

The artifact test test_v61.py verifies the trimming inequality of both cases on 20,000 random padded instances with κ∈(.05,.95)\kappa\in(.05,.95), the width bound (7) for every outcome with t≤104t\leq 10^{4} trials and ζ∈{.025,.05,.25}\zeta\in\{.025,.05,.25\}, and Lemma 4 against constrained numerical optimization.

Consequences.

The ratio of the bounds in parts (i) and (ii) of Proposition 2 is O⁡(d/(κ2​α​(1−α)))O(d/(\kappa^{2}\alpha(1-\alpha))) up to (δ,β)(\delta,\beta) terms. On the uniform sign family, the alternative prior draws of Theorem 5 with r∗​(η)≥α+γr^{*}(\eta)\geq\alpha+\gamma lie in 𝒫γ/2\mathcal{P}_{\gamma/2} by the trimming argument of Theorem 1 (case κ=1/2\kappa=1/2), which uses db≤D≤1/16d_{b}\leq D\leq 1/16; the whole class 𝒫het\mathcal{P}_{\rm het} need not, since trimming a high-risk lower half can lower the risk by more. Hence Theorem 5’s construction also shows that the upper end is attained up to log⁡d\log d there.

Conditioning the priors on the events of Step 2 changes the mixtures by at most their probabilities. A test of level δ\delta over ℋ\mathcal{H} and power β\beta over 𝒫het\mathcal{P}_{\rm het} therefore satisfies

β−δ−β−δ4≤B−0.47+2exp{−Bc∗2/(2L2)},\beta-\delta-\tfrac{\beta-\delta}{4}\leq B^{-0.47}+2\exp\{-Bc_{*}^{2}/(2L^{2})\},

Remarks.

The auditor in this lower bound knows the family, the cells and the exact uniform score marginal; only the location and size of the risk heterogeneity are random. The unknown quantity is a sum of BB nonsmooth terms min⁡{ηb,+,ηb,−}\min\{\eta_{b,+},\eta_{b,-}\}, which is why the argument parallels minimax estimation of ℓ1\ell_{1}-type functionals (Lepski et al., 1999; Cai and Low, 2011; Wu and Yang, 2016).

B.6 Numerical checks for Theorem 5

The script heterogeneity_checks.py (i) computes ELE_{L} by a linear program on a grid; (ii) solves the dual linear program for π0,π1\pi_{0},\pi_{1} and confirms that the optimal moment-matched gap equals 2​EL2E_{L}; and (iii) compares the χ2\chi^{2} series of Step 4 with direct summation over Poisson counts for one group (errors only, which has the same structure with ρ=2​λ/m\rho=2\lambda/m).

Appendix C Estimation complexity, IUT inefficiency, and reference adaptation

C.1 Exact distribution-dependent Rademacher complexity

The profiles of Theorem 2 are distinguished by the population Rademacher complexity, ℜn≍∑bmin⁡{wb,wb/n}\mathfrak{R}_{n}\asymp\sum_{b}\min\{w_{b},\sqrt{w_{b}/n}\}, of order k/n\sqrt{k/n} on a plateau; but it does so at the estimation scale k/γ2k/\gamma^{2}, whereas the optimal audit works at the testing scale k/γ2\sqrt{k}/\gamma^{2}, as in instance-optimal identity testing (Valiant and Valiant, 2017; Balakrishnan and Wasserman, 2019). For ℱw={𝟏Aθ:θ∈{−1,1}B}\mathcal{F}_{w}=\{\mathbf{1}_{A_{\theta}}:\theta\in\{-1,1\}^{B}\} define ℜn​(ℱw)=𝔼S,σ​supθn−1​∑i=1nσi​𝟏Aθ​(Si)\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{w})=\mathbb{E}_{S,\sigma}\sup_{\theta}n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}\mathbf{1}_{A_{\theta}}(S_{i}), with independent Rademacher signs σi\sigma_{i}. Let h⁡(s)h(s) denote the ++/−- half within its group. Since 𝟏Aθ​(s)=(1+θb​h​(s))/2\mathbf{1}_{A_{\theta}}(s)=(1+\theta_{b}h(s))/2 on GbG_{b},

ℜn(ℱw)=12​n∑b=1B𝔼|Zb|,Zb=∑i=1nσih(Si)𝟏{Si∈Gb}.\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{w})=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbb{E}|Z_{b}|,\qquad Z_{b}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}h(S_{i})\mathbf{1}\{S_{i}\in G_{b}\}. (9)

The constant term has expectation zero. A summand in ZbZ_{b} is ±1\pm 1 with probability wb/2w_{b}/2 each, and zero otherwise. Thus, putting v=n​wbv=nw_{b},

𝔼​Zb2=v,𝔼​Zb4≤v+3​v2.\mathbb{E}Z_{b}^{2}=v,\qquad\mathbb{E}Z_{b}^{4}\leq v+3v^{2}.

Hölder’s inequality gives 𝔼​|Zb|≥(𝔼​Zb2)3/2/(𝔼​Zb4)1/2≥v/1+3​v\mathbb{E}|Z_{b}|\geq(\mathbb{E}Z_{b}^{2})^{3/2}/(\mathbb{E}Z_{b}^{4})^{1/2}\geq v/\sqrt{1+3v}, while 𝔼​|Zb|≤min⁡{v,v}\mathbb{E}|Z_{b}|\leq\min\{v,\sqrt{v}\}. Consequently

14​∑bmin⁡{wb,wb/n}≤ℜn​(ℱw)≤12​∑bmin⁡{wb,wb/n}.\frac{1}{4}\sum_{b}\min\{w_{b},\sqrt{w_{b}/n}\}\leq\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{w})\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{b}\min\{w_{b},\sqrt{w_{b}/n}\}. (10)

If n​wmin≥1nw_{\min}\geq 1, this is Θ⁡(∑bwb/n)\Theta(\sum_{b}\sqrt{w_{b}}/\sqrt{n}). For a plateau and n≥kn\geq k, the heavy groups contribute Θ⁡(k/n)\Theta(\sqrt{k/n}) and the residual contributes at most εB/2\varepsilon_{B}/2. Therefore, around n≍k/γ2n\asymp k/\gamma^{2} with εB≤γ/16\varepsilon_{B}\leq\gamma/16, the complexity is of order γ\gamma. Distribution-dependent complexity does distinguish our profiles; it is not one of the quantities matched in Theorem 2.

For indicator policies the squared L2​(P0S)L^{2}(P_{0}^{S}) distance is

∥𝟏Aθ−𝟏Aθ′∥22=∑bwb𝟏{θb≠θb′}.\|\mathbf{1}_{A_{\theta}}-\mathbf{1}_{A_{\theta^{\prime}}}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{b}w_{b}\mathbf{1}\{\theta_{b}\neq\theta_{b}^{\prime}\}.

At any fixed sufficiently small positive resolution, a plateau has logarithmic covering and packing numbers Θ⁡(k)\Theta(k): ignoring residual coordinates gives a 2k2^{k} cover once the squared resolution exceeds εB\varepsilon_{B}, and a constant-relative-distance binary code on the heavy coordinates gives a packing of size exp⁡(c​k)\exp(ck). Thus the usual metric entropy sees the heavy coordinates. The point is a difference between estimation and testing rates, not failure of every distribution-dependent complexity measure.

C.2 Proof of the IUT rate separation

Part (ii) of Theorem 3 is proved for the exact Clopper–Pearson IUT with any fixed positive allocation ζc+ζr=δ\zeta_{c}+\zeta_{r}=\delta. Part (i) is proved for every level-δ\delta EFC audit: on the main range the argument below only uses that the audit does not reject while the constructed policy A^\widehat{A} is empirically feasible, and level δ\delta is used only in the bounded ranges at the end. Constants below may depend on p,δ,βp,\delta,\beta but not on B,k,γB,k,\gamma.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the residual groups, of reference mass ε≤γ/16\varepsilon\leq\gamma/16, with ε=0\varepsilon=0 for k=Bk=B. For a heavy-coordinate sign pattern θH\theta_{H}, define

TH=∑i𝟏{Si∈AθH∖ℛ},WH=∑i(Li−α)𝟏{Si∈AθH∖ℛ}.T_{H}=\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{S_{i}\in A_{\theta_{H}}\setminus\mathcal{R}\},\qquad W_{H}=\sum_{i}(L_{i}-\alpha)\mathbf{1}\{S_{i}\in A_{\theta_{H}}\setminus\mathcal{R}\}.

C.4 Explicit constants when only the loss rate is unknown

Theorem 4 relies on a generic independence tester. When the score marginal is known and uniform, a pilot-and-collision audit gives explicit constants.

Proposition 5 (Adaptation to an unknown constant risk).

On the uniform sign family B=kB=k, let PpP_{p} have uniform scores over the 2​k2k halves and independent L∼Bern⁡(p)L\sim\Bern(p), and let 𝒫a,α,γ={Pp:p∈[a,1−a],p≥α+γ}\mathcal{P}_{a,\alpha,\gamma}=\{P_{p}:p\in[a,1-a],\ p\geq\alpha+\gamma\}. Fix 0<a<1/30<a<1/3, α∈[a,1−2​a]\alpha\in[a,1-2a] and 0<δ<β<10<\delta<\beta<1. For sufficiently small 0<γ≤a0<\gamma\leq a, the audit below has level δ\delta over the unrestricted null, does not take pp as input, and has power β\beta over 𝒫a,α,γ\mathcal{P}_{a,\alpha,\gamma} with Oa,δ,β​(k/γ2)O_{a,\delta,\beta}(\sqrt{k}/\gamma^{2}) samples, which is optimal.

We prove Proposition 5. The score-space partition is known, but the loss probability pp is not an input to the audit. For power, the reference class has uniform scores on the 2​k2k halves and independent L∼Bern⁡(p)L\sim\Bern(p) with p∈[a,1−a]p\in[a,1-a] and p≥α+γp\geq\alpha+\gamma. Type-I validity continues to cover every law in the unrestricted existential null, without uniform-score or score–loss independence assumptions.

Proposition 6 (Singleton experiments are matched).

For a policy AA whose four (𝟏{S∈A},L)(\mathbf{1}\{S\in A\},L) reference cells are positive, the unrestricted singleton testing problem at every sample size is determined by this four-cell law. Hence every member of every sign family has the same singleton minimax complexity.

D.3 Proof of Proposition 7: fixed incidence and VC complexity

For every positive profile, quotient the score space by policy-membership signature. The nonempty signature atoms are exactly the 2​B2B half-groups Gℓ+G_{\ell}^{+} and Gℓ−G_{\ell}^{-}: policy AθA_{\theta} contains precisely GℓθℓG_{\ell}^{\theta_{\ell}} from group ℓ\ell. This 2​B2B-atom incidence matrix depends on BB and the sign labels but not on the mass profile ww. Hence any two profiles have isomorphic quotient set systems; only the reference masses of the atoms differ.

For the VC dimension, choose one point from Gℓ+G_{\ell}^{+} for each of m≤Bm\leq B distinct groups. The corresponding mm membership bits can be set arbitrarily by the mm sign coordinates, so every such mm is shattered and VCdim⁡(𝒜)≥B\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal{A})\geq B. Conversely, among any B+1B+1 points two lie in the same group. If they lie in the same half, every policy gives them identical membership; if they lie in opposite halves, every policy gives complementary membership. In either case the pair cannot realize all four binary labelings, so no B+1B+1 points are shattered. Thus VCdim⁡(𝒜)=B\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal{A})=B.

Finally, for m≤Bm\leq B the shattered construction realizes 2m2^{m} traces. For m>Bm>B, the family contains only 2B2^{B} policies, while an mm-point set containing one point from each Gℓ+G_{\ell}^{+} plus additional distinct points in any already represented half-group still distinguishes all 2B2^{B} sign vectors. Therefore Π𝒜​(m)=2min⁡{m,B}\Pi_{\mathcal{A}}(m)=2^{\min\{m,B\}}.

D.7 Informative nonconstant-reference spectrum

The score-independent reference in Equation (5) is a convenient special case, not a requirement for the separation. The next construction makes the score genuinely informative about risk and makes selective acceptance strictly useful under the reference law.

E.4 Finite-cell Fisher representation

Assume component QkQ_{k} preserves cell masses μj\mu_{j} and has Bernoulli error rate θk,j\theta_{k,j} in cell jj, while P0P_{0} has rate ηj∈(0,1)\eta_{j}\in(0,1). Directly evaluating the two label states shows

Ξ⁡(Qk,Qℓ)=∑jμj​(θk,j−ηj)​(θℓ,j−ηj)ηj​(1−ηj)=∑jμj​gk​(j)​gℓ​(j).\Xi(Q_{k},Q_{\ell})=\sum_{j}\mu_{j}\frac{(\theta_{k,j}-\eta_{j})(\theta_{\ell,j}-\eta_{j})}{\eta_{j}(1-\eta_{j})}=\sum_{j}\mu_{j}g_{k}(j)g_{\ell}(j).
